claim: Muscle spindle Ia afferent firing rates exhibit movement history dependence.
source: Despite decades of research, we lack a mechanistic framework capable of predicting how movement-related signals are transformed into the diversity of muscle spindle afferent firing patterns observed experimentally, particularly in naturalistic behaviors. Here, a biophysical model demonstrates that well-known firing characteristics of mammalian muscle spindle Ia afferents – including movement history dependence, and nonlinear scaling with muscle stretch velocity – emerge from first principles of muscle contractile mechanics.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that movement history dependence is a well-known firing characteristic of mammalian muscle spindle Ia afferents, and this is supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Muscle spindle Ia afferent firing exhibits nonlinear scaling with muscle stretch velocity.
source: Despite decades of research, we lack a mechanistic framework capable of predicting how movement-related signals are transformed into the diversity of muscle spindle afferent firing patterns observed experimentally, particularly in naturalistic behaviors. Here, a biophysical model demonstrates that well-known firing characteristics of mammalian muscle spindle Ia afferents – including movement history dependence, and nonlinear scaling with muscle stretch velocity – emerge from first principles of muscle contractile mechanics.
evidence: The abstract explicitly identifies nonlinear scaling with muscle stretch velocity as a well-known characteristic, and this is demonstrated experimentally and through modeling in the manuscript.

claim: Well-known firing characteristics of mammalian muscle spindle Ia afferents emerge from first principles of muscle contractile mechanics.
source: Here, a biophysical model demonstrates that well-known firing characteristics of mammalian muscle spindle Ia afferents – including movement history dependence, and nonlinear scaling with muscle stretch velocity – emerge from first principles of muscle contractile mechanics.
evidence: This is the primary claim of the study, demonstrated through the biophysical model developed and tested throughout the manuscript.

claim: Alpha drive to muscle and gamma drive to muscle spindle can cause highly variable and complex muscle spindle activity during active muscle contraction and muscle stretch.
source: Further, mechanical interactions of the muscle spindle with muscle-tendon dynamics reveal how motor commands to the muscle (alpha drive) versus muscle spindle (gamma drive) can cause highly variable and complex activity during active muscle contraction and muscle stretch that defy simple explanation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulations presented in Figures 8 and 9, showing how different combinations of alpha and gamma drive produce diverse firing patterns.

claim: Muscle spindle model output can appear to encode aspects of muscle force, yank, length, stiffness, velocity, and/or acceleration depending on neuromechanical conditions.
source: Depending on the neuromechanical conditions, the muscle spindle model output appears to 'encode' aspects of muscle force, yank, length, stiffness, velocity, and/or acceleration, providing an extendable, multiscale, biophysical framework for understanding and predicting proprioceptive sensory signals in health and disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by the various simulations showing how the model can reproduce different encoding properties under different conditions.

claim: Muscle spindle firing patterns do not uniquely encode whole-muscle length and velocity even in tightly controlled experimental conditions.
source: Moreover, manipulations to gamma motor drive reveal that muscles spindle firing patterns do not uniquely encode whole-muscle length and velocity even in tightly controlled experimental conditions (Crowe and Matthews, 1964a; Crowe and Matthews, 1964b; Jansen and Matthews, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Independent activation of alpha and gamma motor neurons can each profoundly alter muscle spindle sensory signals.
source: Independent activation of alpha and gamma motor neurons show that they can each profoundly alter muscle spindle sensory signals, rendering a direct prediction of muscle spindle signals from recordings of movement highly unlikely.
evidence: This claim is supported by both cited literature and the simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Existing computational models of muscle spindle afferent firing have largely been data-driven with phenomenological representations.
source: Existing computational models of muscle spindle afferent firing have largely been data-driven, with well-known experimental features represented phenomenologically (Schaafsma et al., 1991; Hasan, 1983; Lin and Crago, 2002; Mileusnic et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Phenomenological muscle spindle models have high fidelity under the conditions in which data were collected but generalize poorly to more naturalistic conditions.
source: Such models have high fidelity under the conditions in which the data were collected, but generalize poorly to more naturalistic conditions.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior models based on their design principles.

claim: The anatomical arrangement of the muscle and muscle spindle affects the forces on the muscle spindle and alters muscle spindle firing properties.
source: The anatomical arrangement of the muscle and muscle spindle have also been shown in simulation to affect the forces on the muscle spindle and alter muscle spindle firing properties (Lin and Crago, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior simulation work.

claim: The biomechanical properties of intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle have been implicated in determining muscle spindle receptor potentials.
source: The biomechanical properties of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle have also been implicated in determining muscle spindle receptor potentials (Blum et al., 2017; Fukami, 1978; Hunt and Ottoson, 1975; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980; Nichols and Cope, 2004; Poppele and Quick, 1985; Proske and Stuart, 1985), but intrafusal fiber forces have not been recorded experimentally in conjunction with muscle spindle afferent recordings, and only a few recordings of muscle spindle receptor potentials exist (Fukami, 1978; Hunt et al., 1978; Hunt and Ottoson, 1975; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Intrafusal fiber forces have not been recorded experimentally in conjunction with muscle spindle afferent recordings.
source: The biomechanical properties of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle have also been implicated in determining muscle spindle receptor potentials (Blum et al., 2017; Fukami, 1978; Hunt and Ottoson, 1975; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980; Nichols and Cope, 2004; Poppele and Quick, 1985; Proske and Stuart, 1985), but intrafusal fiber forces have not been recorded experimentally in conjunction with muscle spindle afferent recordings, and only a few recordings of muscle spindle receptor potentials exist (Fukami, 1978; Hunt et al., 1978; Hunt and Ottoson, 1975; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing experimental data.

claim: Only a few recordings of muscle spindle receptor potentials exist.
source: The biomechanical properties of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle have also been implicated in determining muscle spindle receptor potentials (Blum et al., 2017; Fukami, 1978; Hunt and Ottoson, 1975; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980; Nichols and Cope, 2004; Poppele and Quick, 1985; Proske and Stuart, 1985), but intrafusal fiber forces have not been recorded experimentally in conjunction with muscle spindle afferent recordings, and only a few recordings of muscle spindle receptor potentials exist (Fukami, 1978; Hunt et al., 1978; Hunt and Ottoson, 1975; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980).
evidence: This is a statement about the scarcity of a particular type of experimental data, supported by citations.

claim: In passive stretch of relaxed rat muscle, muscle spindle Ia afferent firing rates can be described in terms of extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank.
source: We first demonstrated that in passive stretch of relaxed rat muscle, muscle spindle Ia afferent firing rates can be described in terms of extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the experimental work, demonstrated in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: In the relaxed condition, extrafusal muscle fiber forces provide a reasonable proxy for resistive forces of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle mechanosensory apparatus.
source: In the relaxed condition, that is in the absence of central drive to the muscles, we assumed that extrafusal muscle fiber forces provide a reasonable proxy for resistive forces of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle mechanosensory apparatus (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an assumption made for the passive stretch experiments.

claim: Whole musculotendon force in rat experiments is not predictive of muscle spindle IFRs.
source: We previously demonstrated that whole musculotendon force in rat experiments is not predictive of muscle spindle IFRs (Blum et al., 2019), and that only a portion of the total musculotendon force can be attributed to extrafusal muscle fiber force, with the remaining nonlinear elastic component attributed to extracellular tissues (Blum et al., 2019; Meyer and Lieber, 2011; Meyer and Lieber, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors and others.

claim: Only a portion of the total musculotendon force can be attributed to extrafusal muscle fiber force, with the remaining nonlinear elastic component attributed to extracellular tissues.
source: We previously demonstrated that whole musculotendon force in rat experiments is not predictive of muscle spindle IFRs (Blum et al., 2019), and that only a portion of the total musculotendon force can be attributed to extrafusal muscle fiber force, with the remaining nonlinear elastic component attributed to extracellular tissues (Blum et al., 2019; Meyer and Lieber, 2011; Meyer and Lieber, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Fine temporal details of rat Ia afferent firing in relaxed muscles could be reconstructed by linear combinations of estimated extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank, subjected to a threshold.
source: Like in cats (Blum et al., 2017), fine temporal details of rat Ia afferent firing in relaxed muscles could be reconstructed by linear combinations of estimated extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank, subjected to a threshold.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 with experimental data.

claim: Notable features of muscle spindle Ia afferent firing reconstructions include initial bursts, dynamic responses during ramps, rate adaptation during holds, and movement history-dependent firing.
source: The notable features of muscle spindle Ia afferent firing reconstructions included initial bursts, dynamic responses during ramps, rate adaptation during holds, and movement history-dependent firing (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the figures showing model reconstructions of experimental data.

claim: History-dependent initial bursts in Ia afferent firing coincide with large, history-dependent yank component in estimated extrafusal muscle fiber force.
source: The reconstructions revealed history-dependent initial bursts in Ia afferent firing coincide with large, history-dependent yank component in estimated extrafusal muscle fiber force (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B comparing the yank component to the initial burst.

claim: The dynamic Ia afferent firing response during ramp stretches was primarily reconstructed by the force component.
source: The dynamic Ia afferent firing response during ramp stretches was primarily reconstructed by the force component (Figure 2C) and was larger during the first stretch of a repeated sequence (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C showing the force component contribution.

claim: Rate adaptation during the hold period was reconstructed by the force component in both slow and fast stretches.
source: Rate adaptation during the hold period was reconstructed by the force component in both slow and fast stretches (Figure 2C; Matthews, 1963).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Oxaliplatin Ia afferent firing phenotypes were primarily reconstructed by the yank component, with a small contribution of the force component, suggesting a reduced sensitivity of the muscle spindle afferent to intrafusal muscle fiber force.
source: These OX Ia afferent firing phenotypes were primarily reconstructed by the yank component (Figure 2D, blue trace), with a small contribution of the force component (Figure 2D, red trace; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting a reduced sensitivity of the muscle spindle afferent to intrafusal muscle fiber force.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: When Ia afferents in healthy rats were perturbed through intra-axonal electrical stimulation and muscle stretch was applied immediately afterward, STIM Ia afferent firing phenotypes were primarily reproduced by the intrafusal fiber force, with reduced sensitivity to the intrafusal fiber yank.
source: Conversely, when we perturbed the Ia afferent in healthy rats through intra-axonal electrical stimulation (STIM; 500 ms duration, 100 Hz train of 30nA pulses) and applied muscle stretch immediately afterward (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 3), STIM Ia afferent firing phenotypes were primarily reproduced by the intrafusal fiber force, with reduced sensitivity to the intrafusal fiber yank (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The sensitivity of the muscle spindle Ia afferent to force and yank can be decoupled.
source: Taken together, these data show that in the absence of changes in intrafusal or extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank signals, the sensitivity of the muscle spindle Ia afferent to force and yank can be decoupled and therefore may arise due to separate encoding or transduction mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of oxaliplatin and axonal stimulation on force and yank sensitivity.

claim: Varying force- and yank-sensitivity generates diverse muscle spindle firing phenotypes similar to those observed experimentally.
source: Varying force- and yank- sensitivity generated diverse muscle spindle firing phenotypes similar to those observed experimentally – including the OX and STIM phenotypes.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B showing the range of firing patterns produced by varying sensitivities.

claim: Muscle spindle Ia afferent firing profiles exhibited larger initial bursts and dynamic responses as yank sensitivity increased, consistent with classically identified dynamic muscle spindle firing phenotypes.
source: Under passive conditions, muscle spindle Ia afferent firing profiles exhibited larger initial bursts and dynamic responses as yank sensitivity increased (Figure 3B, left to right), consistent with classically identified dynamic muscle spindle firing phenotypes (Emonet-Dénand et al., 1977).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: High force sensitivity led to profiles with elevated plateau firing, consistent with classically-identified static muscle spindle firing phenotypes.
source: High force sensitivity led to profiles with elevated plateau firing (Figure 3B, top to bottom), consistent with classically-identified static muscle spindle firing phenotypes (Emonet-Dénand et al., 1977; Jansen and Matthews, 1962, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: History-dependent muscle forces have been simulated previously based on muscle cross-bridge population cycling kinetics.
source: History-dependent muscle forces have been simulated previously based on muscle cross-bridge population cycling kinetics (Campbell and Lakie, 1998; Campbell and Moss, 2000; Campbell, 2014; Campbell and Moss, 2002), but no current muscle spindle model has incorporated these principles, and thus none simulate history dependence in muscles spindle Ia afferent firing (Hasan, 1983; Lin and Crago, 2002; Mileusnic et al., 2006; Schaafsma et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: No current muscle spindle model has incorporated cross-bridge cycling principles, and thus none simulate history dependence in muscle spindle Ia afferent firing.
source: History-dependent muscle forces have been simulated previously based on muscle cross-bridge population cycling kinetics (Campbell and Lakie, 1998; Campbell and Moss, 2000; Campbell, 2014; Campbell and Moss, 2002), but no current muscle spindle model has incorporated these principles, and thus none simulate history dependence in muscles spindle Ia afferent firing (Hasan, 1983; Lin and Crago, 2002; Mileusnic et al., 2006; Schaafsma et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing models, supported by citations.

claim: Muscle spindles contain bundles of specialized 'bag' and 'chain' intrafusal muscle fibers.
source: Muscle spindles contain bundles of specialized 'bag' and 'chain' intrafusal muscle fibers (Boyd, 1962; Boyd, 1976; Boyd et al., 1977; Gladden and Boyd, 1985; Taylor et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Different intrafusal muscle fibers vary morphologically and mechanically, as well as in their contributions to Ia firing patterns, but their basic architectures are similar.
source: While different intrafusal muscle fibers vary morphologically and mechanically, as well as in their contributions to Ia firing patterns, their basic architectures are similar (Banks et al., 1997; Banks, 2005; Banks, 2015; Gladden and Boyd, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Intrafusal muscle fibers are innervated by gamma motor neurons in two polar regions containing contractile muscle fibers, with an in-series non-contractile equatorial region around which the muscle spindle endings are wrapped and mechanotransduction occurs.
source: Intrafusal muscle fibers are innervated by gamma motor neurons in two polar regions containing contractile muscle fibers, with an in-series non-contractile equatorial region around which the muscle spindle endings are wrapped and mechanotransduction occurs.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about muscle spindle structure.

claim: Muscle spindle Ia receptor potentials and afferent firing are directly related to deformation of the equatorial regions.
source: Muscle spindle Ia receptor potentials and afferent firing are directly related to deformation of the equatorial regions (Boyd, 1976; Boyd et al., 1977), which depends on the tensile forces in intrafusal muscle fibers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mechanistic muscle spindle model consists of a pair of half-sarcomere muscle models arranged in parallel, simulated using two-state actin-myosin population interactions.
source: Our mechanistic muscle spindle model consists of a pair of half-sarcomere muscle models arranged in parallel, simulated using two-state actin-myosin population interactions (Campbell, 2014).
evidence: This describes the structure of the model developed in this study.

claim: The simulated 'dynamic fiber' loosely represented the putative dynamic bag1 intrafusal muscle fibers, thought to mediate muscle spindle initial bursts.
source: The simulated 'dynamic fiber' loosely represented the putative dynamic bag1 intrafusal muscle fibers, thought to mediate muscle spindle initial bursts (Banks et al., 1997; Proske and Stuart, 1985; Schäfer and Kijewski, 1974; Schäfer and Schäfer, 1969; Song et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the model design choice, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The simulated 'static fiber' loosely represented the bag2 and chain intrafusal muscle fibers of the muscle spindle thought to mediate tonic muscle spindle firing.
source: The simulated 'static fiber' loosely represented the bag2 and chain intrafusal muscle fibers of the muscle spindle thought to mediate tonic muscle spindle firing (Figure 4A; Poppele et al., 1979).
evidence: This describes the model design choice, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The dynamic fiber model was designed with slower myosin attachment rates and with a more compliant passive element than the static fiber.
source: The dynamic fiber model was designed with slower myosin attachment rates (Thornell et al., 2015) and with a more compliant passive element than the static fiber (Gladden, 1976) (see Materials and methods; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the model parameters, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mechanistic model predicted a spectrum of muscle spindle firing phenotypes identified in passive stretch conditions by varying the sensitivity (gain) of driving potentials to biophysically predicted intrafusal fiber force and yank.
source: Our mechanistic model predicted a spectrum of muscle spindle firing phenotypes identified in passive stretch conditions by varying the sensitivity (gain) of driving potentials to biophysically predicted intrafusal fiber force and yank (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B.

claim: History-dependent forces emerge within simulated intrafusal muscle fibers from cross-bridge population dynamics.
source: As a result of our chosen kinetic scheme, history-dependent forces emerge within our simulated intrafusal muscle fibers from cross-bridge population dynamics (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C showing the cross-bridge dynamics.

claim: When the muscle is at rest, the spontaneous formation and breakage of cross-bridges is at steady-state equilibrium.
source: When the muscle is at rest, the spontaneous formation and breakage of cross-bridges is at steady-state equilibrium (Figure 4C, time 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C at time point 1.

claim: As soon as a stretch is applied, the population of attached cross-bridges is also stretched, resulting in a short period of high-stiffness force response, known as short-range stiffness.
source: As soon as a stretch is applied, the population of attached cross-bridges is also stretched, resulting in a short period of high-stiffness force response, known as short-range stiffness (Figure 4C, time 2; Lakie and Campbell, 2019).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C at time point 2 and supported by citation.

claim: The scaling properties of muscle spindle dynamic responses and initial bursts with increasing velocity during passive muscle stretch arise from intrafusal cross-bridge kinetics.
source: In our model, the scaling properties of muscle spindle dynamic responses and initial bursts with increasing velocity during passive muscle stretch arise from intrafusal cross-bridge kinetics.
evidence: This is a key finding of the model, demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: The strain dependence of the cross-bridge detachment rates produces force profiles that contain linear increases in short-range stiffness and sublinear increases in force dynamic response as a function of stretch velocity.
source: More specifically, the strain dependence of the cross-bridge detachment rates produces force profiles that contain linear increases in short-range stiffness and sublinear increases in force dynamic response as a function of stretch velocity.
evidence: This explains the mechanism by which the model produces velocity-dependent responses.

claim: The model predicted a sublinear increase in dynamic index with stretch velocity, emergent from intrafusal mechanics, resembling the classically reported fractional-power velocity relationship in muscle spindle firing rates.
source: We predicted a sublinear increase in dynamic index with stretch velocity, emergent from intrafusal mechanics, resembling the classically reported fractional-power velocity relationship in muscle spindle firing rates (Figure 5C; Houk et al., 1981).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Linear scaling of initial burst amplitude with stretch acceleration was predicted.
source: In the same simulations, linear scaling of initial burst amplitude with stretch acceleration was predicted (Schäfer and Kijewski, 1974; Schäfer and Schäfer, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work showing this relationship.

claim: Initial burst scaling was emergent from intrafusal muscle fiber yank at the onset of stretch due to the elasticity of attached cross-bridges that then detach rapidly after being stretched a small fraction of L0.
source: Initial burst scaling was emergent from intrafusal muscle fiber yank at the onset of stretch due to the elasticity of attached cross-bridges that then detach rapidly after being stretched a small fraction of L0 (Hasan and Houk, 1975; Matthews and Stein, 1969).
evidence: This explains the mechanism for initial burst scaling, supported by citations.

claim: Neither fractional-power velocity relationship nor linear acceleration scaling of initial burst has been previously demonstrated to arise from the same mechanistic model.
source: To our knowledge, neither of these phenomena has been previously demonstrated to arise from the same mechanistic model.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model.

claim: The biophysical model predicted history-dependent changes in the muscle spindle firing initial burst and dynamic response analogous to those previously reported in acute cat, rat, and toad experiments as well as in microneurographic recordings in awake humans.
source: Our biophysical model predicted history-dependent changes in the muscle spindle firing initial burst and dynamic response analogous to those previously reported in acute cat, rat, and toad experiments as well as in microneurographic recordings in awake humans (Blum et al., 2017; Day et al., 2017; Haftel et al., 2004; Proske and Stuart, 1985).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: History-dependent features in the model emerged from the asymmetry present in strain-dependent cross-bridge detachment rates.
source: In our model, these features emerged from the asymmetry present in strain-dependent cross-bridge detachment rates.
evidence: This explains the mechanism for history dependence in the model.

claim: In three consecutive, identical stretches, the biophysical muscle spindle model predicted an initial burst and elevated dynamic response on the first, but not second stretch.
source: In three consecutive, identical stretches, the biophysical muscle spindle model predicted an initial burst and elevated dynamic response on the first, but not second stretch (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the third stretch, the amplitude of the simulated driving potentials recovered asymptotically as the time interval between stretches increased to 10 s.
source: In the third stretch, the amplitude of the simulated driving potentials recovered asymptotically as the time interval between stretches increased to 10 s (Figure 6A), resembling the recovery of spike counts during the dynamic response in rats (Figure 6B; Haftel et al., 2004) and the recovery of initial bursts as a function of hold period in toads (Figure 6B; Proske and Stuart, 1985).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and compared to experimental data in Figure 6B.

claim: The model predicted an initial burst at the onset of sinusoidal muscle stretches, similar to that seen in microneurographic recordings from awake humans.
source: Our model predicted an initial burst at the onset of sinusoidal muscle stretches (Figure 6C), similar to that seen in microneurographic recordings from awake humans (Figure 6C; Day et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and compared to experimental data.

claim: A cross-bridge mechanism for history dependence has been proposed previously based on experimental findings.
source: Although a cross-bridge mechanism has been proposed previously based on experimental findings (Haftel et al., 2004; Nichols and Cope, 2004; Proske et al., 1992; Proske and Gregory, 1977; Proske and Stuart, 1985), this is the first demonstration of history dependence in a muscle spindle model.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: This is the first demonstration of history dependence in a muscle spindle model.
source: Although a cross-bridge mechanism has been proposed previously based on experimental findings (Haftel et al., 2004; Nichols and Cope, 2004; Proske et al., 1992; Proske and Gregory, 1977; Proske and Stuart, 1985), this is the first demonstration of history dependence in a muscle spindle model.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model.

claim: Dynamic and static gamma motor neurons innervate the static and dynamic intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle, respectively.
source: Dynamic and static gamma motor neurons innervate the static and dynamic intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle, respectively.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Simulated dynamic gamma drive increased the force and yank of the dynamic fiber during stretch, predicting increased receptor driving potentials underlying initial burst and dynamic responses, with proportionately smaller increases in baseline muscle spindle driving potentials.
source: Consistent with many prior experimental findings, simulated dynamic gamma drive increased the force and yank of the dynamic fiber during stretch, predicting increased receptor driving potentials underlying initial burst and dynamic responses, with proportionately smaller increases in baseline muscle spindle driving potentials (Boyd et al., 1977; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Simulated static gamma drive primarily increased baseline muscle spindle driving potentials, and had much smaller effects on driving potentials underlying the initial burst and dynamic response during stretch.
source: In contrast, simulated static gamma drive primarily increased baseline muscle spindle driving potentials, and had much smaller effects on driving potentials underlying the initial burst and dynamic response during stretch (Figure 7A–B; Crowe and Matthews, 1964a; Boyd et al., 1977; Crowe and Matthews, 1964b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previously reported increases and decreases in dynamic index as a result of dynamic versus static fiber stimulation, respectively, were predicted by the model.
source: Even the previously reported increases and decreases in dynamic index as a result of dynamic versus static fiber stimulation, respectively, (Figure 7C left plot; Crowe and Matthews, 1964a; Crowe and Matthews, 1964b) were predicted by our model (Figure 7C right plot).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When extrafusal muscle was activated to 50% with intrafusal activation at a nominal constant level, the stress in the extrafusal fiber increased, while the stress in the intrafusal fiber decreased.
source: When extrafusal muscle was activated to 50% with intrafusal activation at a nominal constant level, the stress in the extrafusal fiber increased, while the stress in the intrafusal fiber decreased (Figure 8B, first column, top trace, purple and green traces, respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The Ia afferent firing rate simulated using an integrate-and-fire neuron was abruptly silenced during extrafusal muscle contraction when intrafusal activation was held constant.
source: The Ia afferent firing rate simulated using an integrate-and-fire neuron was abruptly silenced during extrafusal muscle contraction (Figure 8B, first column, middle trace); during this condition both the extrafusal and intrafusal muscle lengths decreased and tendon length increased (Figure 8B, First column, bottom trace, green-purple vs. orange trace).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: When intrafusal fiber activation was increased and extrafusal activation was held constant, there was no change in extrafusal stress or force, but an increase in intrafusal stress.
source: In contrast, when intrafusal fiber activation (both static and dynamic) was increased and extrafusal activation was held constant, we observed no change in extrafusal stress or force, but an increase in intrafusal stress (Figure 8B, first column, top trace, purple and green traces, respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The increase in intrafusal stress caused an increased in simulated Ia afferent firing rate with no change in muscle fiber or tendon length.
source: The increase in intrafusal stress causing an increased in simulated Ia afferent firing rate (Figure 8B, second column, middle trace) with no change in muscle fiber or tendon length (Figure 8B, second column, bottom trace).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: When concurrent alpha and gamma drive were simulated, Ia afferent firing was dependent on the relative balance of imposed shortening of intrafusal fibers by alpha drive and the activation of intrafusal fibers by gamma drive.
source: When we simulated concurrent alpha and gamma drive, we observed Ia afferent firing that was dependent on the relative balance of imposed shortening of intrafusal fibers by alpha drive and the activation of intrafusal fibers by gamma drive (Figure 8B, third and fourth columns).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: If the extrafusal muscle shortening caused by alpha motor drive is not sufficiently counteracted by gamma drive, the Ia afferent will reduce its firing rate or cease firing altogether.
source: Briefly, if the extrafusal muscle shortening caused by alpha motor drive is not sufficiently counteracted by gamma drive, the Ia afferent will reduce its firing rate or cease firing altogether (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: If the gamma drive to the spindle stretches the sensory region at a greater rate than the extrafusal shortening, the Ia afferent will increase its firing rate.
source: Alternatively, if the gamma drive to the spindle stretches the sensory region at a greater rate than the extrafusal shortening, the Ia afferent will increase its firing rate (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 8D.

claim: There is a set of extra- and intrafusal states that will lead to no change in Ia firing rate during isometric conditions.
source: Finally, it follows that there is a set of extra- and intrafusal states that will lead to no change in Ia firing rate during isometric conditions (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 8E.

claim: In experiments in human finger muscles, muscle spindle Ia afferents were shown to either increase or decrease their firing rates during an isometric contraction despite the same joint torque profile.
source: We were inspired to use these observations to explain paradoxical Ia afferent firing rates from experiments in human finger muscles (Figure 8C; Edin and Vallbo, 1990), in which muscle spindle Ia afferents were shown to either increase or decrease their firing rates (Figure 8C, bottom traces) during an isometric contraction despite the same joint torque profile (Figure 8C, top traces).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8H and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the absence of gamma drive, the intrafusal fiber stress decreased as alpha drive increased resulting in no muscle spindle firing.
source: As expected, increasing alpha drive decreased extrafusal muscle fiber length (Figure 8B, black trace), and increased extrafusal muscle fiber stress (Figure 8D, purple trace). In the absence of gamma drive, the intrafusal fiber stress decreased as alpha drive increased (Figure 8D, green trace) resulting in no muscle spindle firing as shown experimentally (Elek et al., 1990).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: When gamma drive was increased by a fixed amount, intrafusal fiber stress could increase, decrease, or experience no change in stress depending on the amount of alpha drive.
source: When we increased gamma drive by a fixed amount intrafusal fiber stress could increase (Figure 8D, pink traces), decrease (Figure 8D, green traces), or experience no change (Figure 8D, purple traces) in stress depending on the amount of alpha drive.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D.

claim: It was possible to generate almost any level of muscle spindle firing during isometric conditions where the muscle fibers shorten by varying the relative levels of alpha and gamma drive.
source: As such it was possible to generate almost any level of muscle spindle firing during isometric conditions where the muscle fibers shorten by varying the relative levels of alpha and gamma drive.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulations shown in Figure 8.

claim: When the musculotendon was passive (no alpha drive), the muscle fiber length closely followed the applied musculotendon length.
source: When the musculotendon was passive, i.e. no alpha drive, the muscle fiber length closely followed the applied musculotendon length (Figure 9A, left panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A.

claim: When the extrafusal muscle fiber was activated during the stretch, there was a marked difference in musculotendon length compared to the applied length.
source: Conversely, when the extrafusal muscle fiber was activated during the stretch, there was a marked difference in musculotendon length compared to the applied length (Figure 9A, right panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A.

claim: In the case of the passive spindle, the musculotendon stretch in the absence of alpha drive produced a slightly higher muscle spindle Ia afferent response than in the presence of alpha drive.
source: In the case of the passive spindle, the musculotendon stretch in the absence of alpha drive produced a slightly higher muscle spindle Ia afferent response than in the presence of alpha drive (Figure 9B, top row).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The baseline firing rate, initial burst, and dynamic response were all slightly larger in the case of the passive musculotendon compared to when alpha drive was present.
source: Specifically, the baseline firing rate, initial burst, and dynamic response were all slightly larger in the case of the passive musculotendon.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The addition of a tonic level of gamma drive increased the baseline firing rate, the amplitude of the initial burst, and the dynamic response to stretch in the passive extrafusal musculotendon unit.
source: The addition of a tonic level of gamma drive increased the baseline firing rate, the amplitude of the initial burst, and the dynamic response to stretch in the passive extrafusal musculotendon unit (Figure 9B bottom row, green trace).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Adding alpha drive decreased baseline firing only slightly, abolished the initial burst, and had little effect on the dynamic response to stretch when gamma drive was present.
source: Adding alpha drive decreased baseline firing only slightly, abolished the initial burst, and had little effect on the dynamic response to stretch (Figure 9B bottom row, purple trace).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B.

claim: A diverse range of Ia afferent firing characteristics during passive stretch is emergent from first principles of intrafusal muscle contractile (cross-bridge) mechanisms.
source: We demonstrated that a diverse range of Ia afferent firing characteristics during passive stretch – well-documented in the literature but not completely understood mechanistically – is emergent from first principles of intrafusal muscle contractile (cross-bridge) mechanisms.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Ia afferent firing in a broad range of behaviorally relevant conditions can be reproduced by converting the force and yank of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle into afferent driving potentials using a simple linear relationship.
source: Ia afferent firing in a broad range of behaviorally relevant conditions can be reproduced by converting the force and yank of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle into afferent driving potentials using a simple linear relationship.
evidence: This is demonstrated throughout the manuscript with various simulations.

claim: The transformation from force and yank to driving potentials represents the yet unexplained mechanotransduction process in the equatorial encoding region of muscle spindle sensory organs.
source: This transformation represents the yet unexplained mechanotransduction process in the equatorial encoding region of muscle spindle sensory organs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the model represents.

claim: Mechanical interactions within the muscle-tendon unit and forces external to the muscle all contribute to firing rates of muscle spindle Ia afferents.
source: As such, mechanical interactions within the muscle-tendon unit and forces external to the muscle all contribute to firing rates of muscle spindle Ia afferents; they may even create firing patterns considered to be paradoxical if viewing muscle spindles as simple passive sensors of kinematic or kinetic variables.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulations in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The model provides a foundation for biophysically realistic, predictive muscle spindle models that can be extended to understand how properties of tissues, muscles, neurons, and central drive affect muscle spindle sensory function in health and disease.
source: Importantly, our model provides a foundation for biophysically realistic, predictive muscle spindle models that can be extended to understand how properties of tissues, muscles, neurons, and central drive affect muscle spindle sensory function in health and disease.
evidence: This is a claim about the potential applications of the model.

claim: The approach of starting with biophysical principles of muscle force generation enabled development of a muscle spindle model that predicts nonlinear muscle spindle firing properties beyond the conditions that it was designed to replicate, without any change in model parameters.
source: Our approach of starting with biophysical principles of muscle force generation enabled us to develop a muscle spindle model that predicts nonlinear muscle spindle firing properties beyond the conditions that it was designed to replicate, without any change in model parameters.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling approach and its advantages.

claim: Other muscle spindle models do not exhibit history-dependence and either lack or always generate an initial burst at the onset of stretch.
source: Other muscle spindle models do not exhibit history-dependence and – by design – either lack (Mileusnic et al., 2006) or always generate (Hasan, 1983) an initial burst at the onset of stretch.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior models, supported by citations.

claim: In the model, the initial burst emerges from the number of cross-bridges that are formed after a period of rest, temporarily increasing the stiffness of the fibers before being stretched to their mechanical limit.
source: In our model, the initial burst emerges from the number of cross-bridges that are formed after a period of rest, temporarily increasing the stiffness of the fibers before being stretched to their mechanical limit.
evidence: This explains the mechanism for the initial burst in the model.

claim: The number of cross-bridges formed depends on the prior and current fiber length, velocity, acceleration, and activation of the intrafusal fibers, and thus leads to the modulation of the initial burst of the spindle afferent with these variables.
source: This number depends on the prior and current fiber length, velocity, acceleration, and activation of the intrafusal fibers, and thus leads to the modulation of the initial burst of the spindle afferent with these variables.
evidence: This explains how the initial burst is modulated by different variables in the model.

claim: The fractional power relationship between muscle spindle dynamic responses and stretch velocity has previously been imposed by including it explicitly within the model definition in prior models.
source: Similarly, the fractional power relationship between muscle spindle dynamic responses and stretch velocity (Hasan, 1983; Lin and Crago, 2002) has previously been imposed by including it explicitly within the model definition.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior models, supported by citations.

claim: Prior models fail to account for the history dependence of the velocity sensitivity and thus fail to replicate muscle spindle firing patterns outside of tightly controlled laboratory conditions.
source: While it can be simulated using a phenomenological muscle model with a built-in fractional power function, prior models fail to account for the history dependence of the velocity sensitivity and thus fail to replicate muscle spindle firing patterns outside of tightly controlled laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior models.

claim: History dependence, the nonlinear relationship to stretch velocity, the scaling of the initial burst to acceleration, and firing rate adaptation are all implicit, emergent properties of intrafusal cross-bridge force and yank under different conditions in the model.
source: Here, history dependence, the nonlinear relationship to stretch velocity, the scaling of the initial burst to acceleration, and firing rate adaptation are all implicit, emergent properties of intrafusal cross-bridge force and yank under different conditions – no explicit formulation of these relationships is necessary.
evidence: This is a summary of the emergent properties of the model.

claim: The apparent differential effects on Ia afferent encoding by static and dynamic fusimotor activity are accounted for by the mechanics of muscle force generation.
source: Even the apparent differential effects on Ia afferent encoding by static and dynamic fusimotor activity are accounted for by the mechanics of muscle force generation (Crowe and Matthews, 1964a; Crowe and Matthews, 1964b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7 and supported by citations.

claim: The model was designed with slow cycling myosin in the 'dynamic' fiber and fast cycling myosin in the 'static' fiber, modeled after nuclear bag and chain fibers.
source: We designed our model with slow cycling myosin in the 'dynamic' fiber and fast cycling myosin in the 'static' fiber, modeled after nuclear bag and chain fibers, respectively (Thornell et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the model design, supported by citation.

claim: By taking a structural approach to the interactions between intrafusal and extrafusal muscle fibers, the effect of gamma motor drive were more robustly simulated.
source: By taking a structural approach to the interactions between intrafusal and extrafusal muscle fibers the effect of gamma motor drive were more robustly simulated (Lin and Crago, 2002).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Variations in force and yank sensitivity account for both overall firing characteristics as well as 'static-dynamic' variability across Ia afferents during passive stretch.
source: Variations in force and yank sensitivity account for both overall firing characteristics as well as 'static-dynamic' variability across Ia afferents during passive stretch.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: The few available recordings of muscle spindle receptor potentials during muscle stretch exhibit fast initial transients similar to muscle fiber yank, as well as a sustained potential that resembles muscle force and its decay following a stretch.
source: The few available recordings of muscle spindle receptor potentials during muscle stretch exhibit fast initial transients similar to muscle fiber yank, as well as a sustained potential that resembles muscle force and its decay following a stretch (Hunt and Ottoson, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Sweeping a range of sensitivities to intrafusal force and yank predicts a continuum of firing phenotypes resembling those seen previously in both healthy and perturbed conditions.
source: We show that sweeping a range of sensitivities to intrafusal force and yank predicts a continuum of firing phenotypes resembling those seen previously in both healthy and perturbed conditions (Housley et al., 2020b; Vincent et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 and supported by citations.

claim: Each set of sensitivities can predict muscle spindle firing across different stretch velocities and displacements.
source: Further, each set of sensitivities can predict muscle spindle firing across different stretch velocities and displacements.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulations.

claim: Explicit simulation of the mechanical arrangement of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle-tendon unit enabled demonstration of the profound effects that central drive to alpha and gamma motor neurons can have on muscle spindle firing during active force and muscle stretch conditions.
source: Explicit simulation of the mechanical arrangement of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle-tendon unit enabled us to demonstrate the profound effects that central drive to alpha and gamma motor neurons can have on muscle spindle firing during active force and muscle stretch conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The work emphasizes the importance of modeling the anatomical arrangement of the muscle shown in some prior models.
source: Our work emphasizes the importance of modeling the anatomical arrangement of the muscle shown in some prior models (Lin and Crago, 2002; Mileusnic et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, supported by citations.

claim: With the addition of biophysical force generation mechanics, the model provides a computational testbed to better explore the long-discussed idea that muscle spindle firing rates are driven by properties of intrafusal muscle fiber forces.
source: With the addition of biophysical force generation mechanics we now provide a computational testbed to better explore the long-discussed idea that muscle spindle firing rates are driven by properties of intrafusal muscle fiber forces (Matthews, 1981), and determined by both the central drive to intrafusal and extrafusal muscle fibers, as well as interactions with external forces on the muscle.
evidence: This is a claim about the utility of the model, supported by citation.

claim: When simulating the mechanical interaction of the muscle spindles within the muscle tendon unit, the model reveals that muscle spindle firing can depend critically on the activation, force, and length of the intrafusal fiber within the muscle spindle.
source: When simulating the mechanical interaction of the muscle spindles within the muscle tendon unit, our model reveals that muscle spindle firing can depend critically on the activation, force, and length of the intrafusal fiber within the muscle spindle, which shapes the degree to which muscle spindle firing resembles extrafusal muscle length, velocity, force or other biomechanical variables (Bewick and Banks, 2015; Kruse and Poppele, 1991).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 8 and 9 and supported by citations.

claim: The multiscale model provides a mechanistic framework that can explain the rich diversity of movement-related biomechanical signals in naturalistic behaviors.
source: The multiscale model presented here provides a mechanistic framework that can explain the rich diversity of movement-related biomechanical signals in naturalistic behaviors.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the model's capabilities.

claim: During the swing phase of the cat locomotor step cycle, relaxed ankle extensor muscles are stretched by activity in ankle flexor muscles, and extensor Ia firing rates appear to follow muscle velocity and/or length.
source: For example, the mechanical interactions between intrafusal and extrafusal muscle fibers (Figures 8 and 9) may explain the complex relationships between Ia afferent signals in locomotion to muscle length and force. During the swing phase of the cat locomotor step cycle, relaxed ankle extensor muscles are stretched by activity in ankle flexor muscles, and extensor Ia firing rates appear to follow muscle velocity and/or length (Prochazka and Gorassini, 1998a; Prochazka and Gorassini, 1998b), which closely resemble extrafusal and intrafusal muscle force and yank (Blum et al., 2017) in passive conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ia afferent firing rates during swing phase closely resemble extrafusal and intrafusal muscle force and yank in passive conditions.
source: During the swing phase of the cat locomotor step cycle, relaxed ankle extensor muscles are stretched by activity in ankle flexor muscles, and extensor Ia firing rates appear to follow muscle velocity and/or length (Prochazka and Gorassini, 1998a; Prochazka and Gorassini, 1998b), which closely resemble extrafusal and intrafusal muscle force and yank (Blum et al., 2017) in passive conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The same muscle spindle Ia afferent fires in early stance when there is no change in muscle length, but the muscle is both active due to alpha drive, and loaded due to carrying the weight of the animal.
source: However, the same muscle spindle Ia afferent also fires in early stance when there is no change in muscle length, but the muscle is both active due to alpha drive, and loaded due to carrying the weight of the animal: this firing is likely due to intrafusal force resulting from the interactions between gamma drive, alpha drive, and the external load (Figure 8, green traces).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental observations based on the model.

claim: The same muscle spindle afferent ceases firing in midstance, when the intrafusal muscle is possibly activated by gamma drive, but not enough to prevent the muscle spindle from falling slack as the extrafusal muscle fiber shortens due to alpha drive.
source: The same muscle spindle afferent ceases firing in midstance, when the intrafusal muscle is possibly activated by gamma drive, but not enough to prevent the muscle spindle from falling slack as the extrafusal muscle fiber shortens due to alpha drive (Ellaway et al., 2015; Prochazka, 2015; Prochazka and Gorassini, 1998b; Figure 8, purple traces).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental observations based on the model, supported by citations.

claim: Ia afferent firing has been shown in humans to be highly dependent on resistive loads applied to an attempted movement.
source: Ia afferent firing has been shown in humans to be highly dependent on resistive loads applied to an attempted movement (Dimitriou, 2014; Edin and Vallbo, 1990; Vallbo, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In coupled agonist-antagonist systems, Ia afferents under alpha-gamma coactivation or beta motor control signal the effects of loads on a joint originating outside their parent muscles.
source: An interpretation of this observation could be that, in coupled agonist-antagonist systems, Ia afferents under alpha-gamma coactivation or beta motor control signal the effects of loads on a joint originating outside their parent muscles.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of experimental observations.

claim: Simulating intermuscular interactions is likely necessary to predict proprioceptor activity during movement.
source: Simulating such intermuscular interactions is likely necessary to predict proprioceptor activity during movement, and would require multiple muscle and muscle spindle models to be coupled.
evidence: This is a speculation about future modeling needs.

claim: The core framework provides proof of concept for more elaborate and biophysically accurate model of muscle spindle firing necessary to predict muscle spindle signals during naturalistic movement conditions in health and disease.
source: The core framework presented provides proof of concept for more elaborate and biophysically accurate model of muscle spindle firing necessary to predict muscle spindle signals during naturalistic movement conditions in health and disease.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance and potential of the model.

claim: The model can be used as a platform to enable the development of computational models capable of testing the effects of a wide variety of multiscale mechanisms on muscle spindle firing.
source: Importantly, our model can be used as a platform to enable the development of computational models capable of testing the effects of a wide variety of multiscale mechanisms on muscle spindle firing, including architectural arrangement of the muscle spindle within the muscle (Maas et al., 2009), intra- and extrafusal muscle myosin expression, more complex muscle force-generating mechanisms, extracellular matrix stiffness, mechanosensory encoding mechanisms, and biophysical neural dynamics that could all be affected by aging and disease.
evidence: This is a claim about the potential applications of the model.

claim: The primary focus in developing the mechanistic model was to use the simplest two-state cross-bridge model of actin-myosin interactions to qualitatively reproduce history dependence in its stretch responses.
source: Our primary focus in developing our mechanistic model was to use the simplest two-state cross-bridge model of actin-myosin interactions to qualitatively, but not quantitatively, reproduce history dependence in its stretch responses (Figure 6A) as seen in biological Ia afferents (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach.

claim: Despite discrepancies in the more abrupt stretch-shorten 'triangle' stretches, the model was able to closely reproduce the human Ia afferent response during the slow sinusoidal stretch.
source: It should be noted that, despite the discrepancies in the more abrupt stretch-shorten 'triangle' stretches (Figure 6A), our model was able to closely reproduce the human Ia afferent response (Figure 6B,C) during the slow sinusoidal stretch, which may be more physiologically relevant.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of model limitations and successes.

claim: With the modeling approach, it is impossible to separate the elastic contributions from endomysial tissue from those in myofilaments, from structures such as titin.
source: With our approach, it is impossible to separate the elastic contributions from endomysial tissue from those in myofilaments, from structures such as titin.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the modeling approach.

claim: It may be necessary to account for muscle-specific kinetic schemes or to replace the simple linear model of titin with more sophisticated properties to capture calcium-dependent hysteresis in regulation of titin stiffness and a range of other complex processes of muscle force generation.
source: It remains to be seen which aspects of complex muscle spindle properties will improve the model's predictive capabilities, but it may be necessary to account for muscle-specific (Campbell, 2014) kinetic schemes or to replace the simple linear model of titin with more sophisticated properties (Nishikawa et al., 2012) to capture calcium-dependent hysteresis in regulation of titin stiffness and a range of other complex processes of muscle force generation (Campbell, 2016; Campbell, 2017; Mann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation about future model improvements, supported by citations.

claim: Additional sources of history-dependence could include history dependence in extrafusal muscle fibers and non-contractile tissues, or the inertial of the muscle mass when rapidly accelerated.
source: Additional sources of history-dependence could include history dependence in extrafusal muscle fibers and non-contractile tissues, or the inertial of the muscle mass when rapidly accelerated.
evidence: This is a speculation about other potential mechanisms.

claim: The model may have failed to account for the complex process(es) responsible for the occlusion between multiple transduction zones in the primary afferent.
source: Another possibility is that we failed to account for the complex process(es) responsible for the occlusion between multiple transduction zones in the primary afferent (Banks et al., 1997; Mileusnic et al., 2006), in which the firing rate may be more dependent on the bag1 fiber during the initial stretch and become more dependent on to bag2 and chain fibers in later stretches.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential limitation, supported by citations.

claim: A comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms underlying muscle spindle mechanotransduction remains elusive.
source: A comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms underlying muscle spindle mechanotransduction, that is, translation of mechanical stimuli to receptor potentials, remains elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Lacking sufficiently detailed information from the literature, the entire neuromechanical transduction process was represented by a set of constant gains.
source: Lacking sufficiently detailed information from the literature, we represented the entire neuromechanical transduction process by a set of constant gains.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a simplification in the model.

claim: The dynamics of yet uncharacterized viscoelastic properties of the equatorial regions of intrafusal muscle fibers, ion channels in muscle spindle afferent endings, and intrinsic neural dynamics of the afferent plays a significant role in the resulting muscle spindle firing signals.
source: However, we do recognize that the dynamics of yet uncharacterized viscoelastic properties of the equatorial regions of intrafusal muscle fibers, ion channels in muscle spindle afferent endings (Bewick and Banks, 2015; Carrasco et al., 2017), and intrinsic neural dynamics (e.g. those underlying neural history dependence, spike-frequency adaptation, and occlusion Banks et al., 1997) of the afferent plays a significant role in the resulting muscle spindle firing signals.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of factors not fully captured in the model, supported by citations.

claim: The anatomical arrangement of the model could also provide a biophysical framework for understanding muscle spindle group II afferents that are located at the junction between the polar and equatorial regions of intrafusal muscle fibers, as well as Golgi tendon organ Ib afferent located at the extrafusal musculotendinous junction.
source: Finally, we focused only on the muscle spindle Ia afferent, but the anatomical arrangement of our model could also provide a biophysical framework for understanding muscle spindle group II afferents that are located at the junction between the polar and equatorial regions of intrafusal muscle fibers, as well as and Golgi tendon organ Ib afferent located at the extrafusal musculotendinous junction.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential extensions of the model.

claim: It would be beneficial to adopt the approach of Mileusnic et al., 2006 and optimize the parameters of the model to match the careful experimental conditions of specific muscles and animal models.
source: In future studies, it would also be beneficial to adopt the approach of Mileusnic et al., 2006 and optimize the parameters of our model to match the careful experimental conditions of specific muscles and animal models.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work, supported by citation.

claim: The complex interplay between central drive, internal, and environmental forces cannot be ignored when decoding muscle spindle firing patterns, especially in voluntary movement and during interactions with the environment.
source: Ultimately, it is clear that the complex interplay between central drive, internal, and environmental forces cannot be ignored when decoding muscle spindle firing patterns, especially in voluntary movement and during interactions with the environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling work.

claim: Neuromechanical interactions are key in interpreting the afferent signals and percepts in a variety of conditions where mismatches in extrafusal and intrafusal mechanical state due to fatigue or pre-conditioning alter the perception of both force and position.
source: Such neuromechanical interactions are key in interpreting the afferent signals and percepts in a variety of conditions where mismatches in extrafusal and intrafusal mechanical state due to fatigue or pre-conditioning alter the perception of both force and position (Proske et al., 2014; Proske and Gandevia, 2012), or the role of muscle spindles in perception of force and weight (Jami, 1992; Luu et al., 2011; Savage et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The multiscale biophysical model provides a new biophysical framework to move beyond the idea that muscle spindles can be characterized as simple passive encoders of biomechanical signals during movement.
source: Our multiscale biophysical model provides a new biophysical framework by which we may move beyond the idea that muscle spindles can be characterized as simple passive encoders of biomechanical signals during movement, enabling a more sophisticated understanding of muscle spindles as proprioceptive sensors, their role in neural control of movement, and how neurological disorders disrupt sensorimotor systems.
evidence: This is a summary of the significance of the work.
